units.summary: A shepherd denies receiving animals entrusted to him without witnesses, but after witnesses testify he ate them, Rabbi Zeira rules that the plaintiff must take the oath to collect payment since the shepherd is a proven robber.

Two people argue over the ownership of a bathhouse, and one of them attempts to resolve the stalemate by consecrating the property to the Temple. Two people dispute ownership of a bathhouse until one consecrates it, leading the local rabbis to avoid the facility and Rabba to seek a ruling in Sura.
A dispute over a bathhouse is referred from Rav Ḥisda to Rav Huna and finally to Rav Naḥman, who resolves it using a specific legal principle.
While traveling on a ship, Rabban Gamliel realizes he has not separated his tithes and proceeds to transfer ownership of them to the Elders traveling with him.
Rabbi Abba travels to Sura and recounts his legal debate with Ulla to the local scholars.
Avuh bar Ihi bought a loft from his sister, but after a creditor seized it, Shmuel ruled he could not recover his money because no property guarantee was written.
Shmuel instructs his scribe, Rav Ḥinnana bar Sheilat, to include specific compensation clauses in deeds of sale if the parties agree.
The Gemara reports that Shmuel would regularly collect payments from buyers for land enhancements to satisfy creditors.
The Sages send Rav Sheshet's objection to Rabbi Abba bar Zavda, who dismisses it as simple, prompting Rava to argue that it is actually very deep.
An incident occurred in Pumbedita where a court ruling was challenged by Sages, leading to a sharp exchange between Rav Yosef and Abaye regarding the validity of the objection.
Rav Nahman recalls witnessing a public announcement by the judges in Mar Shmuel's court during his childhood regarding the return of found deeds.
Shabbtai son of Rabbi Marinus pledged a wool cloak to his daughter-in-law but denied it when her marriage contract was lost, only to be contradicted by witnesses.
Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba questions Rabbi Yoḥanan's legal innovation, and Rabbi Yoḥanan responds with a metaphor about uncovering hidden truths.

A bill of divorce is found in Rav Huna's court with specific geographic identifiers, leading to a discussion on whether it should be returned. Rav Hisda warns Rabba that Rav Huna will question him in the evening, prompting Rabba to go out and research the law.
Rabba issued a ruling regarding a bill of divorce found in a flax house in Pumbedita.

Rabba bar bar Hana loses a bill of divorce in the study hall and has it returned based on his identification, later wondering which legal principle was applied. Rabba bar bar Ḥana loses a bill of divorce in the study hall and successfully retrieves it by providing identifying marks.
The Gemara deliberates on the legal status of returning lost wills and deeds of gift based on whether the giver was healthy or on their deathbed.

A bill of divorce is found in Rav Huna's court, leading to a discussion and investigation into whether it can be returned to its owner. Following a legal debate regarding a found bill of divorce, a cedar beam in the study hall breaks, leading the involved sages to attribute the event to the offense caused by their sharp words.
Ameimar, Mar Zutra, and Rav Ashi visit an orchard where a sharecropper offers them fruit, leading to a dispute over whether they are permitted to eat it without the owner's explicit consent.
A man finds pitch and hesitates to keep it despite Rav's ruling, so Rav tells him to give half to Rav's son Hiyya to demonstrate his confidence in the ruling.
Mar Zutra identifies a thief by observing a student's disregard for another's property, leading to the recovery of a stolen silver goblet.
A man finds four dinars in the Biran River and is told by Rav Yehuda to proclaim the find despite the location.
Rav Yehuda follows Shmuel through the grain market and asks him about the law regarding a found purse.
Rava follows Rav Naḥman through the tanner's market and asks about the status of a found purse.
A kite drops stolen meat in a specific grove, and Abaye permits the finder to keep it.
Rabbi Ḥanina finds a slaughtered goat on the road and the Sages permit him to keep it.
Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Yitzḥak Nappaḥa find slaughtered birds on the road and are permitted to keep them.
Rav Nahman explains a legal ruling regarding a lost coin among three people using a hypothetical scenario of despair (ye'ush).
A legal discussion regarding whether a finder must return a coin based on the number of people present when it fell, determining the likelihood of owner despair.
Rava categorizes the various biblical prohibitions violated depending on when and with what intent a person picks up a lost coin.
Rava rules that if one finds a coin dropped in sand, they are not obligated to return it because the owner likely despaired immediately.
Rabbi Ami finds a purse of dinars and is seen by a Roman who, noticing his fear of the law, tells him to keep the find for himself.
The father of Rav Pappa lost a donkey, and after it was found, Rabba bar Rav Huna required him to bring witnesses to his integrity before allowing him to reclaim it.
Raḥava approaches Rav Yosef to ask if he may use orphan money in his possession, prompting a legal challenge from Abaye.
While sitting before Rabba, Abaye throws a clod at some goats, leading Rabba to rule that Abaye has now initiated the act of returning a lost item and must complete it.
Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei repeatedly buys and declares ownerless a man's bundle of wood to fulfill the commandment of assisting him without compromising his own dignity as an elder.
Rav Safra unilaterally divides a partnership venture he shared with Issur and seeks legal validation for the act from Raba bar Rav Huna.
Shmuel rent his garment in mourning for a Sage who had explained a single specific law to him, demonstrating his definition of a primary teacher.
When Rav Hisda asked Rav Huna a question about the status of a student who is also a peer, Rav Huna took offense and rebuked him, leading to a forty-year rift between them.
During the time of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, students abandoned the Mishna for the Talmud, prompting him to publicly teach that they should return to prioritizing the Mishna.
The Sages consult the experts of the school of Rabbi Ḥiyya and Rabbi Oshaya to determine if two baraitot were originally taught as a single unit.
A man who claimed to have lost deposited jewels had his property seized by Rav Nachman to pay the debt, but when the jewels were later found, the property was returned to him.
A group of gardeners who usually left their tools with an old woman changed their routine one day, leading to a theft and a subsequent ruling by Rav.
Rav Sheshet rules on a case in Neharde'a regarding a captive's property, but Rav Amram challenges his textual proof, leading to a sharp verbal exchange.
An old woman and her daughter are taken captive, and after the woman's death is confirmed, Abaye and Rava determine how to divide her estate among her surviving daughter and a grandson.

Mari bar Isak denies his long-lost brother's claim to their father's estate until Rav Hisda intervenes and witnesses eventually confirm the brother's identity. A legal dispute between Mari bar Isak and his long-lost brother escalates between the courts of Rav Hisda and Rabbi Ami until Rabbi Ami concedes upon learning the brother is a minor.
The Gemara cites a brief incident where a jug burst due to the expansion of grain during the rainy season to support a physical claim.
A man deposited money with a bailee who stored it in a willow hut, and after it was stolen, Rav Yosef ruled that the storage was negligent regarding fire.
A bailee claimed he forgot where he stored a deposit, and Rava ruled that such a claim constitutes negligence.
A bailee entrusted a deposit to his mother, who stored it in a chest from which it was stolen, leading Rava to deliberate on the liability.
A man entrusted money to a friend who gave it to his mother for safekeeping; she put it in a chest from which it was stolen, leading Rava to rule on their liability.
A steward bought an ox for orphans and gave it to a cowherd, but the ox died because it had no teeth to eat, leading to a dispute over liability.
A brewer mistakenly used a depositor's hops instead of the bailee's hops to make beer, resulting in a legal debate when the beer spoiled.
Rabbi Zeira instructs Rabbi Abba bar Pappa to travel via the Ladder of Tyre to ask Rabbi Ya’akov bar Idi about Rabbi Yoḥanan's ruling on Rabbi Akiva's opinion.
Rabbi Shimon challenges his father, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, for teaching a law differently in his old age than he had taught it in his youth.
Rav borrows gold dinars from Rabbi Ḥiyya's daughter and, after their value increases, is told by Rabbi Ḥiyya to repay the actual coins rather than their original silver value.

Rav Pappa transferred ownership of twelve thousand dinars located in Bei Ḥozai to his agent Rav Shmuel bar Aḥa using a legal artifice involving his house's threshold, and the agent successfully retrieved the money.
Levi searches through his collection of baraitot and finds a text supporting the view that money effects acquisition in the context of consecrated property.
Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Yosef tries to renege on a salt sale after the price rises, but Rabbi Yoḥanan rules that he must fulfill the entire deal or submit to the 'He Who exacted payment' curse.
Rav Kahana receives money for linen but the price rises, leading Rav to rule on how much of the verbal agreement he must fulfill.
Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Matya's son hires laborers and promises them food, but his father instructs him to retract the offer before they start working.
A man pays for sesame, but the sellers renege when the price rises; the buyer refuses to take his money back, and it is subsequently stolen.
A man buys wine but tries to cancel the deal after hearing the vizier's men intend to seize it, leading to a ruling by Rav Hisda.
Rabbi Tarfon issues a lenient ruling in Lod that initially makes the merchants happy, but they later realize it hurts them and ask to return to the previous standard.
Rami bar Ḥama encounters his landlord who is sad over a bad donkey sale and advises him to retract the transaction.
A man selling silk strips sets a price, and a buyer calculates whether the price constitutes exploitation.
A man selling jewelry sets a price, and a buyer calculates the exploitation involved.
Rami bar Ḥama is unable to resolve a series of legal dilemmas regarding the fifth-payment, so the matter is brought to Rava who provides a scriptural derivation.
A Tanna recites a baraita regarding the redemption of non-kosher animals before Rabbi Elazar, who then questions the logic of the baraita's exclusions.
A tanna recites a teaching about the severity of public humiliation before Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak, who confirms the teaching based on physiological observation.

The famous 'Oven of Akhnai' narrative where Rabbi Eliezer's rejection of the majority's legal authority leads to his ostracism, cosmic upheaval, and the eventual death of Rabban Gamliel through the prayers of Eliezer's wife.
Rava received wine from a shop, diluted it, found the taste unsatisfactory, and returned it to the store.
An elderly slave dyes his hair to appear young and get purchased by Rav Pappa bar Shmuel, only to wash the dye off later to claim he is too old to serve.
Ravina visits Sura and engages in a theological and legal discussion with Rav Hanina regarding the mention of the Exodus in the context of creeping animals.
Rabbi Yehuda cites an incident where Baitos ben Zunin sold his field following Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's instructions, allowing the buyer to eat the produce.
Rav Kahana recounts sitting in the study hall and hearing Rav repeat a cryptic phrase about gourds, which he later asks the students to explain.
Rav Yosef bar Ḥama seized and worked the slaves of his debtors, leading his son Rava to challenge the legality of the practice based on the laws of interest.
A man sells land without a guarantee and, seeing the buyer's distress, promises to compensate him if the land is seized, leading to a rabbinic discussion on the validity of such a promise.
A dying man writes a divorce for his wife to spare her legal complications but sighs in grief, leading his wife to promise she will remain his if he survives.
After Rav Nahman rules in favor of a lender in the Exilarch's court, Rav Yehuda physically tears up the document in protest, leading to a sharp verbal exchange about legal authority.
A man sells land with a guarantee for high-quality reimbursement, but after his best land is sold, the rabbis debate whether he must provide his remaining best land or only intermediate quality.
Rav bar Shabba pledges wine to Rav Kahana if a debt isn't paid on time, leading Rav Pappa to consider if the laws of asmakhta apply to movable goods.
A woman sends an agent to buy land from her relatives, and during the sale, the agent gives an ambiguous verbal commitment to allow the seller to buy it back.
Ravina acted in a case by removing the value of consumed produce from a lender.
Rav Ashi performed a legal action regarding the property of orphans.
Mar son of Ameimar describes to Rav Ashi how his father would record projected profits in loan documents but would later reduce the debt if the borrowers reported that no profit was actually made.
A business document involving the late Rav Ilish is brought before Rava, who interprets its ambiguous terms favorably to ensure no prohibition of interest was violated.
Rav Elazar of Hagronya sets up a fattening arrangement with his sharecropper, which is then questioned by the sharecropper's wife, leading to a discussion on the nature of their partnership.
Rav Menashya bar Gadda unilaterally divides offspring from a joint venture and is rebuked by Abaye for doing so without proper authorization.

Two Samaritans engage in two separate disputes over unilateral division of assets (money then wine) before Rav Pappa, who distinguishes between the two cases. Rav Pappa explains to two Samaritans why he ruled differently in their dispute over money versus their dispute over wine.
Rav Hama rented out currency for a fee, believing it was like renting a tool, but he eventually lost all his money as a punishment.
Abba Mar would receive wax from manufacturers in exchange for his father, Rav Pappa, lending them money, leading the Sages to challenge the practice as interest.

Rav Anan cites the specific practice of Mar Shmuel, who managed a copper kettle belonging to the orphans of Mar Ukva by weighing it before and after rentals to collect both rent and depreciation fairly.

A man whose orchard was being extorted by a lender cleverly transferred the property to his son before 'selling' it to the lender, leading to a legal dispute over the validity of the sale and the status of the funds paid.
Rav pays donkey drivers to bring wheat from a cheaper market (Kafri) to Sura, assuming the risk of transport to avoid usury issues.

Passage B is a distinct incident where Rava provides proactive legal advice to field guards, whereas Passage A is a separate event where Rava defends his own personal business practices against the Rabbis' accusations.
The Rabbis accuse Rava of taking interest by waiting longer to collect from sharecroppers, but he argues his method is actually more ethical than theirs.

Rav Mari bar Rahel attempts to pay rent to Rava for a house Rava bought from a gentile who had mortgaged it to Rav Mari, but Rava refuses the payment based on the legal standing of the original mortgage.
Passage B introduces new actors (Rava of Barnish and Rav Ashi) and a completely different legal subject (prepayment for wine vs. real estate mortgages) compared to Passage A.
Ravina regularly receives extra wine from his suppliers and questions Rav Ashi on whether this constitutes interest or if the suppliers even own the land they work.

This is a distinct incident involving different actors (Rav Pappa and Rava) and a different legal subject (head tax and labor vs. land tax and wine), following the same structural pattern as the previous story.
Rav Se’oram would press people who behaved improperly into service as Rava's sedan chair carriers, an act Rava justified with a baraita.
Ameimar would pay for clay only once it was brought into his house, which the Gemara analyzes to determine which Tanna he follows.
A man acting as an agent for his father-in-law pays for jewelry whose price then drops, leading to a dispute brought before Rav Pappa regarding which price applies.
Rav Ashi tests Ravina's adherence to the law by requesting a loan at a busy time without witnesses, but Ravina refuses to lend the money until witnesses and a contract are prepared.
A Tanna recites a law regarding laborer wages before Rav, who corrects him by citing a different ruling from his uncle, Rabbi Ḥiyya.
A man sells a donkey but remains unpaid by one dinar, leading him to repeatedly seek payment and prompting Rav Ashi to deliberate on whether the sale is finalized.
A man reports seeing rot on the king's clothing and is executed after being interrogated about the specific material he saw it on.
A man took a donkey to sell it on the condition that he would return it if unsuccessful, but the donkey was injured during the return journey, leading to a legal dispute.

A worker asked his colleagues to watch his cloak while he baked for them, but it was stolen; Rav Pappa initially held them liable but was embarrassed when the legal status of the owner's labor was questioned.

Rav Pappa rules against a group of workers for a stolen cloak, is embarrassed when challenged on legal grounds, but is vindicated when it is discovered the owner was drinking beer rather than working at the time.
A tall man and a short man swap clothes to cross a river, the tall man's sheet is lost, and Rava's initial ruling is challenged until the specific nature of the swap is revealed.
A man rents a donkey and ignores the owner's warning about which path to take, leading to the donkey's death and a subsequent legal debate between Rava and Abaye.
A man breaks a barrel in the Mehoza market and Rava instructs him to bring witnesses to prove it was an accident.
After Rabba bar bar Hanan seizes the cloaks of porters who broke his wine barrel, Rav intervenes and compels him to return the garments and pay their wages based on ethical standards.
Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Matya's son hires laborers with a vague promise of food, leading the father to intervene and specify the terms to avoid an impossible obligation.
Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon is appointed as a thief-catcher for the government, executes a man who insulted him, and later undergoes a miraculous surgery to confirm his own righteousness.

The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei also served in a similar capacity as a government officer. Elijah the Prophet encounters Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei and urges him to flee his role as a government informant, just as his father had done.
A Roman noblewoman mocks the extreme obesity of Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Elazar, questioning how they could father children, and they provide a sharp retort.
Rabbi Yoḥanan habitually sits outside the ritual bath so that women will see his beauty and have beautiful children, dismissing the Rabbis' concerns about the evil eye.

The tragic saga of Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish, from their first meeting at the Jordan River to their fatal falling out over a legal dispute and Rabbi Yoḥanan's subsequent descent into madness. The Gemara recounts the later life, suffering, death, and miraculous post-mortem preservation of Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon in his attic before his eventual burial.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi proposes to Rabbi Elazar's widow but is rejected because she considers him spiritually inferior to her late husband.
A flashback explains the academic rivalry between Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, starting from their youth in the study hall and a controversial seating demotion.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, inspired by Rabbi Elazar's suffering, accepts thirteen years of physical ailments upon himself.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's suffering begins when he shows no mercy to a calf being led to slaughter and ends years later when he prevents his maidservant from harming small weasels.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi redeems the wayward son of Rabbi Elazar b. Shimon by ordaining him and placing him under the tutelage of a scholar, eventually leading him to become a renowned sage.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi finds the wayward grandson of Rabbi Tarfon and successfully incentivizes his repentance by offering his daughter's hand in marriage.
Rav Yosef undertakes series of forty-day fasts to ensure that Torah knowledge will remain within his family for generations, receiving dream-confirmations after each set.
Upon moving to Eretz Yisrael, Rabbi Zeira performs hundreds of fasts to purge his previous style of learning and to gain spiritual protection.
Rabbi Zeira regularly tests his holiness by sitting in a hot oven, but one day the envy of the Sages causes him to be burned, resulting in a permanent nickname.
Reish Lakish attempts to mark the burial cave of Rabbi Hiyya but is unable to find it, leading him to feel unworthy and pray to God.

Passage B introduces new actors (Rabbi Hanina and Rabbi Hiyya) and a distinct narrative conflict regarding the preservation of Torah, independent of Reish Lakish's search for the burial cave in Passage A.

Passage B features a distinct set of actors (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabbi Yishmael) and a specific dialogue-based encounter that evaluates the preceding events, constituting a separate narrative unit.
Passage B is a distinct dream narrative involving Rabbi Zeira and Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina, whereas Passage A is a separate account involving Rav Haviva and a different anonymous Sage.
A sage is blinded by fire after looking at Rabbi Hiyya's heavenly chariot but is healed after praying at Hiyya's burial cave.
Elijah reveals the power of Rabbi Hiyya's prayer to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, leading to a near-messianic event that is stopped by heavenly decree and Elijah's intervention.
Shmuel the physician heals Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's eye through an indirect method, but despite the Rabbi's efforts, Shmuel cannot be ordained because it was not his destiny.
Rabba bar Nahmani flees royal persecution, is summoned to resolve a legal dispute in the heavenly academy, and dies while declaring a ruling of purity.
Rabbi Shimon ben Halafta, being obese and hot, sits on a rock and asks his daughter to fan him for a reward.

Rabbi Yohanan ben Matya's son hires laborers and stipulates their food, leading to a discussion on the limits of such stipulations. Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Matya's son hires laborers with a food stipulation, leading his father to intervene and clarify that they are only entitled to local custom to avoid impossible obligations.
During the intense heat following his circumcision, Abraham sends Eliezer to find guests and eventually goes himself, leading God to send angels to visit him.
To silence scoffers who claimed Isaac was a foundling, Abraham and Sarah hosted a feast where Sarah miraculously nursed the children of all the guests.
The Gemara recounts how Abraham, Jacob, and Elisha prayed for the introduction of aging, illness, and recovery into the world to provide social order and preparation for death.
The members of Rav Pappa bar Abba's household approached Rav Pappa with two legal questions, and he provided them with restrictive rulings.
Rav Ashi relates a legal inquiry he received from the Exilarch's household regarding the prohibition of crossbreeding animals in a single pen.
Rav finds a hidden scroll in Rabbi Hiyya's house containing a radical ruling by Isi ben Yehuda and expresses his concern that it would destroy people's livelihoods.
The page consists of a legal deliberation regarding whether a laborer's right to eat produce belongs to him or to Heaven, analyzed through various hypothetical cases and baraitot.
A shepherd whose animal drowned in the Pappa River is exempted from liability by Rabba because the incident was unavoidable.
The conclusion of a case where a shepherd's animal drowned and Rabba exempted him because it was beyond his control.
Bar Adda the porter is held liable by Rav Pappa after an animal he was transporting across a narrow bridge pushed another into the river.
Aivu deposited flax which was stolen by Shabbu; Rav Nahman later held the bailee liable once the thief was identified.
A hypothetical case is discussed regarding a shepherd who claims to be protected but then has an animal stolen.
Rav Aha and Ravina debate whether a borrower is liable for negligence when the owner is present.
A man borrows an ax that breaks and Rava tells him to bring witnesses to be exempt from payment.
Rav remains silent when challenged on his ruling regarding a broken ax, and the Gemara concludes the law follows his challengers.
A man borrows a pail that breaks and Rav Pappa rules he is exempt if he brings witnesses of proper use.
The Rabbis attempt to use Rava's ruling to exempt themselves from liability to him, causing Rava to become angry and refute them.
Mareimar bar Hanina helps his renters load a mule which then dies; Rava initially rules the renters liable but is embarrassed when the Rabbis point out the owner was present during the work.

A man initially refuses to pay for trees planted in his field without permission, but after Rav observes him fencing and guarding them, Rav rules that his actions demonstrate his approval and he must pay the higher value.
A man who could not find storage for his wine betrothed a woman specifically so she would grant him access to her courtyard for his goods.
A baraita alludes to a tragic incident involving a man who took his mezuza with him when vacating a rented house.

A specific dispute arose in Tzippori over the rent of a bathhouse during a leap year due to contradictory language in the rental agreement. A dispute over rent for an intercalated month in Tzippori is brought before Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Yosei, who rule that the parties must split the cost.

When the children of Alexandrian women whose mothers were snatched at their weddings came to Hillel to determine their legitimacy, he examined the marriage contracts and found a clause that retroactively validated the second marriages.
Ravina writes a large sum in his daughter's marriage contract and refuses the groom's family's request for a formal act of acquisition to solidify it.
A man on his deathbed instructs his heirs to give a sum to his daughter, leading to a rabbinic inquiry into his linguistic intent.
A sharecropper promises a high penalty if he neglects land, neglects a third of it, and the Sages of Nehardea rule on his liability.
A sharecropper plants wheat instead of sesame, and Rav Ashi rules that he doesn't get extra credit for saving the land's strength because owners prefer immediate profit.
A sharecropper plants wheat instead of sesame and produces a surplus, leading to a rabbinic disagreement over how to split the extra profit.
A man leased land for garlic by a river that subsequently dried up, leading Rava to rule that he was exempt from payment despite a Mishnaic ruling to the contrary.
A tenant who was supposed to grow hay grew barley instead; when the barley failed, Ravina ruled he could not pay with the blighted crop because the land had already fulfilled its original mission.
A man's wine turned sour after harvest, and Rav Ashi ruled that he could not pay his lease with it because the damage occurred to the product, not the land.
Rav Yehuda and Ravin bar Rav Naḥman, who owned adjacent fields, agreed to share the fruit of their trees that leaned over each other's boundaries.
Rabbi Abba meets the students of Rav and they exchange different interpretations of biblical blessings regarding the location of one's house and property.
Rav visits a cemetery and performs a ritual or inspection to determine that ninety-nine out of a hundred people died due to the evil eye.
Rav Natan bar Hoshaya cuts down sixteen cubits of trees along a riverbank and is subsequently attacked by the residents of Mashronya.
Rabba bar Rav Huna is asked to cut down his trees on the riverbank but refuses to do so until his neighbors, including a powerful general, cut theirs first.
Rabba bar Rav Naḥman cuts down a forest belonging to Rabba bar Rav Huna to clear a river path, leading the latter to unknowingly curse him, resulting in the death of Rabba bar Rav Naḥman's children.
Rav Pappa, acting as a contractor for hay, demands payment for palm trees that sprouted in the field, leading to a debate with Rav Sheisha over the nature of the loss and enhancement.
Rav Beivai bar Abaye builds a fence on contracted land and later demands payment for trees that sprouted there, only to be rebuked by Rav Pappi.
After his planter dies leaving five sons-in-law, Rav Yosef attempts to remove them from the land to prevent potential negligence.
A planter stipulates he will leave if he ruins the vineyard, and when he does cause a loss, Rav Yehuda and Rav Kahana debate his right to compensation for existing enhancements.
Runya, a planter for Ravina, is fired for causing a loss and unsuccessfully appeals to Rava, who justifies the dismissal.
A planter requests his share of a field's enhancement so he can move to the Land of Israel, and Rav Pappa bar Shmuel rules in his favor.
A man mortgages an orchard that withers halfway through the term, leading to a dispute over whether the wood is considered principal or produce.
A creditor and debtor dispute the length of a mortgage, and the creditor preemptively consumes the orchard's fruit while the case is pending.

Yehuda bar Mareimar, Mareimar, and Mar Zutra employed specific hiring strategies, such as hiring each other or using specific language with attendants, to ensure they did not violate the prohibition against delaying wages.

Rabba bar Avuh encounters Elijah the Prophet in a gentile cemetery and asks him whether the court makes arrangements for a debtor's basic needs. Rabba bar Avuh meets Elijah, who takes him to Paradise to gather leaves to alleviate his poverty, but after a heavenly voice rebukes him for consuming his reward in the World-to-Come, he discards the leaves yet still gains wealth from the miraculous scent left on his cloak.
A man takes a slaughtering knife as collateral and is ordered by Abaye to return it because it is a vessel used for food preparation.
In Nehardea, goats ate someone's barley, leading the owner of the barley to seize them and receive a ruling from Shmuel's father.
Rava physically removed a pair of wool-cutting scissors and a book of Aggada from the possession of orphans based on the principle that such items are typically lent.
A man sold a vine supported by a peach tree, and after the tree was uprooted, the case was brought before Rabbi Yitzḥak to determine the buyer's rights.
An incident occurred where the floor of an upper story broke, causing water from the upper resident's washing to leak onto the resident below.
Efrayim the scribe reports that when Rabbi Shimon's ruling was presented to King Shapur, the King offered him high praise.
